column1: Goals|Which learning outcome most clearly describes an observable performance?|Compare two research designs and justify a choice|Understand everything|Appreciate all knowledge automatically|Become perfect at research|An observable outcome states a performance for which evidence can be collected; compare and justify are assessable actions.

Goals|Why should assessment align with learning outcomes?|The task should elicit the capability the outcome describes|Every assessment must use the same format|Assessment can replace teaching entirely|Outcomes should be hidden from learners|Alignment connects goals, teaching opportunities and evidence; recall alone does not establish application or evaluation.

Goals|Which task mainly requires application?|Use a known formula to solve a new relevant problem|Repeat a memorized definition verbatim|Copy the title of a chapter|List only page numbers|Application uses knowledge in a situation rather than merely reproducing its wording.

Goals|Which task mainly requires evaluation?|Judge two explanations against stated evidence and criteria|Copy both explanations|Count the words without interpreting them|Repeat a heading|Evaluation involves a justified judgment using relevant criteria and evidence.

Methods|When is a demonstration especially useful?|When learners need to observe a process before practising it|When every learner must remain passive permanently|When no process is involved|When all questions must be prohibited|A demonstration makes a process visible; guided and independent practice are still needed to develop competence.

Methods|What is a useful role of a case study in teaching?|Connect principles with the analysis of a contextual situation|Guarantee that one case represents every possible situation|Remove the need for evidence|Replace all concepts with anecdotes|Case studies support contextual analysis, but generalization requires care and additional evidence.

Methods|What is an appropriate reason to use small-group discussion?|Learners can articulate, compare and revise their reasoning|It guarantees every group agrees|It makes monitoring unnecessary|It ensures no learner needs prior knowledge|Discussion benefits from clear goals, participation expectations and feedback rather than merely placing people together.

Methods|What is the key feature of problem-based learning?|Learning organized around investigating a meaningful problem|Repeating a solution without inquiry|Removing all guidance|Using only multiple-choice tests|Learners identify what they need to know and investigate a problem with appropriate facilitation.

Methods|Which classroom arrangement supports active learning?|Learners explain, practise and evaluate ideas with feedback|Learners only listen in every session|Learners never encounter challenge|Learners only copy slide text|Active learning involves meaningful cognitive participation, not movement or technology alone.

Methods|Why is prior knowledge important when introducing a concept?|It influences how new information is interpreted|It makes learning impossible|It is identical for every learner|It replaces every new example|Teachers should elicit prior knowledge and misconceptions so that new ideas can be connected or contrasted effectively.

Methods|What is a useful purpose of questioning after a lecture segment?|Check reasoning and adjust the next instruction|Publicly embarrass uncertain learners|Only fill remaining time|Avoid hearing alternative views|Questions should gather evidence of understanding and support responsive teaching.

Methods|How should technology be chosen for instruction?|By its contribution to a learning goal and accessibility|Only by novelty|Only by price|Only by the number of animations|A tool is useful when it supports learning and participation; technology use alone does not establish effectiveness.

Assessment|Which assessment use is formative?|Using current responses to plan targeted feedback|Reporting only a final degree classification|Issuing a final certificate without feedback|Ranking institutions by enrolment alone|Formative use guides improvement while learning is in progress; the purpose matters more than the instrument's name.

Assessment|Which assessment use is summative?|Reporting achievement at the end of a defined course|Adjusting tomorrow's explanation after an exit ticket|Diagnosing a misconception before instruction|Giving practice feedback without a final judgment|Summative assessment summarizes achievement over a completed learning period.

Assessment|What is a criterion-referenced interpretation?|Judging performance against defined standards|Judging performance only against other candidates|Using handwriting size as the only criterion|Ignoring stated learning goals|Criterion-referenced decisions compare evidence with specified criteria rather than a group's ranking distribution.

Assessment|What is a norm-referenced interpretation?|Comparing a score with a relevant reference group's performance|Comparing only with a fixed mastery checklist|Guaranteeing mastery from a high rank|Ignoring the comparison population|Norm-referenced meaning depends on the reference group; rank and mastery are not interchangeable.

Assessment|Why is an explicit scoring rubric useful?|It clarifies criteria and performance levels|It guarantees all raters always agree without training|It removes the need to inspect work|It proves every score is valid|Rubrics support transparent judgments and feedback; rater interpretation and evidence still matter.

Assessment|What is item difficulty in a basic test-analysis context often summarized by?|The proportion answering the item correctly|The number of letters in the question|The paper's printing cost|The teacher's preference|A high correct-response proportion means an item was easier for that tested group; difficulty depends on the population.

Assessment|What does an item discrimination measure seek to examine?|How responses distinguish levels of overall performance|Only the number of answer options|Only the size of the font|Only the examination date|Discrimination concerns the relationship between item performance and an appropriate overall performance measure.

Assessment|What should a teacher do before interpreting a low score as lack of knowledge?|Check access barriers, task alignment and relevant evidence|Assume a permanent inability|Ignore all contextual information|Treat the score as a complete description of the person|Language, accessibility, unclear instructions or misaligned tasks can affect scores as well as knowledge.

Research|What is a research problem?|A focused issue or question to investigate|A guaranteed final answer|Only the report's cover colour|Only the researcher's title|A well-defined problem guides objectives, design, evidence and interpretation.

Research|What is a literature review intended to do?|Critically synthesize relevant prior work and identify context or gaps|Copy every source without citation|Guarantee no new evidence is needed|List titles without examining them|A literature review connects existing evidence, methods and debates to the new research question.

Research|What is an operational definition?|A specification of how a concept will be observed or measured|A dictionary entry used without measurement choices|A final conclusion before data collection|A list of all unrelated variables|Operationalization makes the measurement procedure explicit so that others can interpret and examine it.

Research|Which variable is deliberately manipulated in a controlled experiment?|Independent variable|Dependent variable|Every confounder automatically|Only the participant's name|The independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured as an outcome.

Research|Which variable is measured as an outcome in an experiment?|Dependent variable|Independent variable|Only the sampling frame|Only the report title|The dependent variable records the response whose relationship to the manipulated factor is being investigated.

Research|What is a confounding variable?|A factor related to the studied variables that can provide an alternative explanation|A synonym for the final result|A factor guaranteed to be irrelevant|A variable that never changes|Confounding can distort an apparent relationship; design and analysis should address plausible alternative explanations.

Research|Why does random assignment help an experiment?|It reduces systematic group differences in expectation|It guarantees groups are identical in every observed characteristic|It makes measurement unnecessary|It is identical to random sampling|Random assignment distributes participants among conditions. It differs from sampling participants from a population.

Research|What is random sampling primarily concerned with?|How members are selected from a population|How participants are assigned to treatments|How fonts are chosen|How a conclusion is announced|Sampling determines inclusion in a study; assignment determines conditions after inclusion.

Research|What is the population of a study?|The defined group about which the investigation seeks conclusions|Only the people who replied first|Only the researcher|Only the list of final variables|The population must be defined so that sampling and the scope of conclusions can be assessed.

Research|What is a sampling frame?|The list or operational source from which a sample is selected|The report's page border|The final sample mean|A guarantee of complete population coverage|A frame can omit or duplicate population members; coverage affects representativeness.

Research|What is convenience sampling?|Selecting participants mainly because they are readily available|Giving every member an equal known selection probability|Assigning treatments randomly|Selecting only by a complete census|Convenience samples can be useful but may differ systematically from the intended population.

Research|What is stratified sampling?|Sampling within defined subgroups of a population|Selecting only the largest city|Using only volunteers without grouping|Assigning every participant the same treatment|Stratification divides a population into defined strata and samples within them according to a planned design.

Research|What is a census?|Collecting information from every member of a defined population|Studying only one randomly chosen person|Repeating one interview indefinitely|Assigning participants to experimental groups|A census seeks full population coverage, although nonresponse and measurement errors can still occur.

Research|What is a major limitation of a cross-sectional study?|It observes a snapshot rather than following change within individuals over time|It can never describe any pattern|It always proves causation|It needs no sampling decisions|Cross-sectional designs examine a period or point in time; longitudinal data address change more directly.

Research|What is a longitudinal study?|A design collecting information over time from relevant units|A study with a long title|A study using only one moment's data|A study with no repeated measurement|Longitudinal designs help examine change but require attention to timing, attrition and repeated-measurement effects.

Research|What does correlation establish by itself?|An association between variables|A guaranteed causal mechanism|Proof that confounding is impossible|Proof that both variables are identical|Association alone does not identify causal direction or rule out alternative explanations.

Research|What is a pilot study useful for?|Testing procedures and feasibility before the main study|Guaranteeing the final hypothesis is correct|Replacing all main-study data in every case|Avoiding informed consent|Piloting can reveal unclear instruments, recruitment difficulties and operational problems.

Research|Why should missing data be reported and examined?|Missingness can affect conclusions and may not be random|Missing values are always zero|Missingness always proves dishonesty|Removing records always eliminates bias|Patterns and reasons for missing data influence interpretation and the appropriateness of methods used to handle them.

Research|What does replication seek to do?|Examine whether findings can be obtained again under appropriate conditions|Repeat citations without collecting evidence|Guarantee no uncertainty exists|Publish identical wording under a new name|Replication checks robustness and reproducibility; differences in conditions and methods should be reported.

Research|What is triangulation in research?|Using multiple sources or methods to examine a question|Drawing three unrelated diagrams|Replacing evidence with three opinions|Assuming all methods always agree|Triangulation can reveal convergence or discrepancies, each of which needs interpretation.

Ethics|What is plagiarism?|Presenting another person's ideas or words as one's own without appropriate acknowledgment|Quoting with clear attribution|Reporting one's own observations honestly|Disagreeing with a cited source|Cite borrowed ideas as well as words; changing a few words does not remove the need for attribution.

Ethics|What is fabrication in research?|Inventing data or observations|Correcting a documented typographical error|Reporting limitations|Using an approved questionnaire|Fabrication creates evidence that was not obtained and undermines the validity of the work.

Ethics|What is falsification in research?|Manipulating or omitting material so that the record misrepresents the research|Reporting a null finding|Explaining a method|Correcting an error transparently|Falsification distorts the record rather than honestly representing what was done and found.

Ethics|Why is informed consent important?|Participants need relevant information and a voluntary choice|Consent permits every future undisclosed use|Consent removes the need for confidentiality|Consent guarantees the study's hypothesis|Consent supports autonomy and does not replace other ethical obligations.

Ethics|What is the difference between anonymity and confidentiality?|Anonymous data cannot readily identify individuals; confidentiality controls disclosure of identifiable information|They always mean publishing all names|Confidentiality means no data are collected|Anonymity guarantees no risk in every situation|Anonymity and confidentiality are distinct protections; indirect identifiers and context can still create risks.

Ethics|Why should data collection follow a minimization principle?|Collect only information needed for the stated purpose|Collect every possible personal detail|Publish raw identifiers by default|Avoid defining a research question|Unnecessary personal information increases risk without necessarily improving the study.

Writing|What is a suitable structure for explaining a research method?|Describe design, participants, measures and procedures sufficiently to examine the work|List only the author's qualifications|Present only a preferred conclusion|Hide sampling decisions|Transparent methods allow readers to assess what evidence was obtained and whether it supports the claims.

Writing|Why should a research report discuss limitations?|Readers need to judge the scope and uncertainty of conclusions|Limitations always make research worthless|Limitations are the same as fabricated data|They replace reporting results|Limitations clarify what the design and evidence can and cannot establish.

Writing|What is a justified response when results do not support a hypothesis?|Report the results honestly and examine their implications|Invent supporting observations|Remove all inconvenient records without explanation|Change the conclusion without reporting the evidence|A hypothesis is tested against evidence; unsupported results should be reported rather than concealed.

Writing|What is the purpose of citing a source in academic writing?|Acknowledge contributions and let readers trace evidence or ideas|Guarantee the cited claim can never be questioned|Replace the writer's reasoning entirely|Increase word count without relevance|Citations support attribution and traceability; authors still need to assess quality and relevance.
